brand_breakdown.format: Brand Breakdown #{n}. Data: pull {brand}'s live ads (India unless noted) from the public Meta Ad Library the Friday before (Apify ads-library actor via the terminal, about $1-3 a pull), have AI read every ad, then fill each slide with real counts. Never use a number that isn't from the pull. Say plainly what public data can't show (spend, ROAS, dark ads; long-running isn't the same as winning, clients raised this). Market: {market}. Format follows the reference post the user shared (account split, sameness, what's lasting, what they get right, what to question, hooks with run times, takeaway, caveats), as a carousel. Caption: 2-line hook with the most surprising count, 3-4 short lines, link-free, Follow Galvor.
slides: [cover] {brand} is running [N] Meta ads. We read every one.
[stat] Who posts them: brand page vs creator partnership ads
[list] How alike they are: captions reused, top openers, CTA mix, language mix
[stat] What's lasting: ads live 30+ days (a likely winner, not proof)
[list] Three hooks and how long each has run
[statement] The takeaway for a brand your size
[text] How we did this: public Meta Ad Library, [date range]. No spend or ROAS data; run time is a proxy.
[cta] Follow Galvor for a new brand every Tuesday

client_stories.title: 'Brand fit' is a word agencies hide behind
client_stories.hook:
"Brand fit is a very loose word."
A bank's marketing head told us that. He has a point.
client_stories.body:
His point was simple. Every agency deck says the creators are a great brand fit. Nobody can tell him what that means, and in the end he's the one who decides anyway.

So we've stopped using the word with clients. We ask them to write fit down as things you can check instead.

Do they speak on camera, and in which language?
Is their audience 27 to 45, or mostly college kids?
Have they done a rival brand in the last six months?
Anything in their past that'll come up in the comments?

Written like that, two people can look at the same creator and agree. You can also argue with it, which is kind of the point.

If your brief just says brand fit, the agency fills in the meaning for you. Usually with whoever has the most followers.
client_stories.source: BFSI marketing head, calls 10 Aug and 12 Oct 2026; a hair-care brand said the same on 4 Jun

client_stories.title: A 250K creator now costs more than a 1M one
client_stories.hook:
A 250K creator now costs more than a 1M one.
Two fashion brands told us this in the same month.
client_stories.body:
One said the same creators had put their rates up by about half in two or three months. The other said smaller creators were quoting more than people with four times the followers.

At first it sounds broken. I don't think it is.

A 1M account often has a huge audience that never buys anything. The 250K creator has people who actually trust them. They know that, so they charge for it.

Rate cards are slowly moving from reach to believability. Brands still negotiating on follower count will keep overpaying for the wrong people, and losing the right ones to someone who pays properly.

Before agreeing a fee I'd look at two things. How their sponsored posts do next to their normal ones. And what the comments say when they recommend something.
client_stories.source: Menswear D2C (26 Aug) and an ethnic-wear retailer (13 Oct 2026); numbers are the brands' own

client_stories.title: Shortlist 20, sign 10, get 5 videos
client_stories.hook:
Shortlist 20 creators. Sign 10. Get 5 videos.
And half of those 5 can't be used.
client_stories.body:
That's not a made-up funnel. A menswear brand walked us through their last few campaigns and it went roughly like that every time.

Some creators went quiet after onboarding. A couple took three or four months to deliver. One launch slipped by a month because briefing ran late.

Everyone measures the top of that funnel. How many creators did we find, how many did we sign. Almost nobody tracks how many usable videos came out the other end, or what each usable one really cost.

Do that maths once and it changes how you shortlist. You stop picking 20 people who look good and start picking 10 who'll deliver what you asked for, on time.

Try it for one campaign. It's a bit painful, but worth it.
client_stories.source: Menswear D2C, call 26 Aug 2026 (their own numbers)

client_stories.title: "We're drowning in numbers. Most of them are rubbish."
client_stories.hook:
"Most of our numbers are rubbish."
That's from a marketing head at a big company. Not me.
client_stories.body:
He said his real job is deleting numbers, not getting more of them. He wants a few that tell him a story and tell him what to do next.

We've heard some version of this from nearly every brand we showed a dashboard to this year. One asked, what do I actually tell my team on Monday? Another wanted the top 10 changes per market and nothing else.

We got this wrong for a while. Our first dashboards had too much in them, because more felt like more value.

Now the first page is a short list of things to change, each with the ad it came from. The charts are still there, just further down, for whoever wants them.

If you're planning 2027 reporting this week, try cutting the weekly report in half. See who notices.
client_stories.source: BFSI marketing head (10 Aug); nutrition and hair-care brands (Aug-Nov 2026)

client_stories.title: 400 leads. Zero bookings.
client_stories.hook:
400 leads. Zero bookings.
And the ads weren't the problem.
client_stories.body:
A hospitality brand told us about their last agency. Cheap leads, lots of them, not one booking. Each booking was worth a lot, so this hurt.

When we looked, the ad was fine. Everything after it wasn't.

The button sent people to an Instagram profile. There were no questions to check if someone was actually planning a trip. And replies went out hours later, because the sales team works office hours and leads don't.

So the agency was judged on cost per lead, delivered cheap leads, and technically did its job.

Before you judge an ad, follow one lead the whole way. Click it yourself, fill the form, wait for the reply. Most of the time you'll find the leak in ten minutes.
client_stories.source: Hospitality brand, call 14 Oct 2026; an edtech launch (11 Sep) had the same break after the form

client_stories.title: Your best Tamil ad is invisible
client_stories.hook:
Your best Tamil ad is invisible.
The national dashboard averaged it away.
client_stories.body:
A hair-care brand said this to us, more or less. Something works really well in Kerala and badly up north, and the overall number calls it average.

They spend a small amount in one southern state. Too small to ever show up in a national report, but a big deal for that market.

Nobody actually thinks India is one market. Yet most creative reporting still rolls everything into one table.

What's helped the brands we work with: review each region on its own. Fewer ads per region, sure, but the patterns you find are real.

And check who writes the regional brief. A lot of Tamil briefs are written in English and the creator translates on the fly. One brand told us that's exactly what they do, because nobody on the team reads Tamil.
client_stories.source: Hair-care D2C (18 and 27 Aug), kids' nutrition brand (15 Oct 2026)

client_stories.title: Cheap creators, expensive ads
client_stories.hook:
Cheap creators plus a big boost budget.
For one brand, that ended up costing more.
client_stories.body:
An apparel brand had gone mostly nano and micro. Lower fees, more creators, more money left over for ads behind the posts. Makes sense on paper.

Once real ad money went behind those videos, the bigger creators, 50K and up, came out cheaper per result. What they saved on fees went straight back out as ad spend.

I'm not saying small creators don't work. Some kinds of video did fine at that size, testimonials for one.

But if you're paying Meta to push the video anyway, the creator fee is the small number. What matters is how the video does once you pay for reach.

So add it up properly. Fee plus boost, per result. Not just the fee.
client_stories.source: Fashion D2C, call 11 Nov 2026 (Galvor analysis of their creator ads)

client_stories.title: "Influencer marketing is a waste of money"
client_stories.hook:
"Influencer marketing is a waste of money."
A CMO who's run brands and agencies told us that.
client_stories.body:
He's been through agency after agency. Every one promised reach. A lot of it was fake, or the right people never saw it.

Honestly, I'd say the same if that was my experience.

But what failed for him was the buying, not the channel. Creators picked on follower count, paid for organic reach that never showed up, judged on views.

The brands we see getting it right do it differently. They screen hard first, and most creators don't make it through. They pay for the content, then put ad money behind the videos that work. And they judge it on sales, like any other ad.

Done that way it's just another source of creative. A good one, usually.

client_stories.title: "Help me prove brand ads to my management"
client_stories.hook:
"Help me prove brand ads to my management."
That's all a head of digital asked us for.
client_stories.body:
Their company runs two ad teams. One for performance, one for brand. Performance has ROAS and everyone gets it. Brand has a feeling that it's helping.

They can see branded searches go up. People talk about them online. Store traffic moves. But they can't say these five customers came because of that ad, so the brand budget is always the one being questioned.

I don't have a clean answer, and I don't trust anyone who says they do. Attribution is messy and will stay messy.

What I'd do: before the campaign, write down a few things that should move if brand ads work. Branded search, direct traffic, repeat buyers. Check them after. Not perfect, but a lot better than arguing on gut feel.
client_stories.source: Ethnic-wear retailer's digital head, call 13 Oct 2026

client_stories.title: 10 videos a month for Rs 5,000
client_stories.hook:
A CMO makes 10 videos a month for Rs 5,000.
Making content isn't the hard part anymore.
client_stories.body:
He showed us. A promo video that used to take him a full day takes about ten minutes now.

So what's actually scarce? Knowing what to make.

A new brand we spoke to had three ads live and was copying what its competitors ran. Totally understandable. But copy the category's winners long enough and you end up sounding exactly like the category.

When anyone can make a hundred videos, the brands that win know which ten to make. That comes from your own results, not your competitors'.
client_stories.source: Fractional CMO (1 Oct) and an edtech launch (11 Sep 2026)

client_stories.title: Most marketing teams are one tired person
client_stories.hook:
Most brand marketing teams are one tired person.
Most marketing tools are built for ten.
client_stories.body:
A founder in the UK told us his marketing is the bare minimum. He's on his own, so he uses Claude for most of it. No shame in that.

A footwear brand said it from the other side. You can't expect a senior person to spend eight hours a week reading data.

When we started, we built for a big team with an analyst. Most of the brands we work with don't have one.

So now the first question we ask is: what's the one problem you'd fix this month if you could? We start there, and only there.

If you're that one person, don't try to fix everything at once. Pick one thing.
client_stories.source: UK food brand founder (21 Oct), footwear D2C (26 Aug 2026)

client_stories.title: Lead count looked fine for eight months
client_stories.hook:
Lead count looked fine for eight months.
Lead quality didn't.
client_stories.body:
A founder told us he'd handed his ads to an outside campaign manager. He checked the top number every week. Leads were coming in, so it all seemed fine.

Junk leads were creeping up the whole time. By the time he noticed, the account he'd built over years was a mess.

Nobody lied to him. He was just watching the number that's easiest to show.

If someone else runs your ads, ask them for one number that's hard to make look good. For him it should have been leads that turned into a real conversation.

client_stories.title: Plan on the sponsored number, not the average
client_stories.hook:
Same creator. Same followers.
Their sponsored posts get about half the engagement.
client_stories.body:
We see this all the time. One creator we checked for a retail brand did around 7% on normal posts and under 4% on brand deals.

That's normal. People know when it's an ad. A fashion brand put it bluntly: everyone knows the content they're seeing is paid.

The problem is which number goes into the plan. Most plans use the creator's average engagement, and that's mostly their normal posts.

Use their last few sponsored posts as the baseline instead.

It makes the forecast less exciting. It also makes it right.
client_stories.source: Galvor Scout run shown on a Gulf retailer call (6 Oct 2026); fashion D2C quote (11 Nov)

client_stories.title: The creator for your Android launch loves their iPhone
client_stories.hook:
You book a creator for an Android launch.
They've been praising their iPhone for two years.
client_stories.body:
A retail team asked us this exact question. A phone brand wants three creators. How do you know none of them has spent two years talking up a rival?

Bios won't tell you. Agency lists won't either. You only find out by watching what they've posted.

Same with logos. We once flagged a rival brand's shoes clearly visible in a creator's draft. Nobody on the shoot had noticed.

This is where AI is actually useful. It can watch hundreds of a creator's videos and check what's on screen, what they say and what's in the captions. A person can't do that for 40 creators before a deadline.

Add one line to your next brief: no rival products shown or praised in the last six months. Then actually check it.

client_stories.title: 15 creators, great awareness, 2 sold
client_stories.hook:
15 creators. Great awareness.
Two of them actually sold anything.
client_stories.body:
A streetwear brand told us this. Lots of views, plenty of clicks, nothing in the cart.

When you go ad by ad, the clicks are often fine. The problem is further down.

For a different brand, one creator's audience was mostly parents of newborns, and the product was for toddlers. Decent click rate, poor sales, high cost. Right creator, wrong audience.

In another case the clicks never turned into page views. That's the landing page or stock, not the video.

"The creator didn't work" is usually three or four different problems. Split it into hook, click, page and buy, and you'll know which one to fix.
client_stories.source: Streetwear D2C (19 Nov 2026); kids' nutrition analysis (19 Oct and 19 Nov)

client_stories.title: The bio says fashion. The reels say gym.
client_stories.hook:
The bio says fashion.
The last 30 reels are gym videos.
client_stories.body:
A brand told us this about creators their agency suggested. Another got a creator recommended for "speaks Bihari" because a database said so. Nobody had watched a single video.

Most creator tools work off metadata. Bio, category tags, follower count, maybe a guessed location. Quick, and often wrong.

The only reliable way is to watch the videos. What do they talk about? Do they speak on camera? In which language? Who's in the comments?

That used to be impossible at scale. Now AI watches around 20 recent videos per creator before anyone sees the shortlist.

It still gets things wrong sometimes. But it's wrong about what they actually post, not about their bio.
client_stories.source: Streetwear D2C (19 Nov); creator network call (21 Oct 2026)

client_stories.title: Our dashboard told a brand to cut long ads. It was wrong.
client_stories.hook:
Our dashboard told a brand to cut long ads.
Their best ad was 45 seconds of a mum talking.
client_stories.body:
This one's on us.

We'd built a rule from lots of accounts: show the product early, long ads lose people. Usually true.

Then a nutrition brand showed us their top two ads. One was a mum talking for 40-odd seconds. The other was a doctor with a long intro before the product even appears. On cost per new customer, both were winning.

Their buyers are parents, and parents watch for the information. The general rule just didn't fit how they buy.

So we changed two things. We split new customers from retargeting, and we stopped judging ads that hadn't spent enough to judge.

If a tool's advice doesn't match what you know about your buyers, push back. We needed that.

client_stories.title: "Can't I just build this in Claude?"
client_stories.hook:
"Can't I just build this in Claude?"
Honestly? Most of it, yes.
client_stories.body:
We hear this a lot now. One brand had already connected their Meta ads to Claude before we met them. Another wrote a script in ChatGPT that beat ours. It did, we checked.

So I don't think the answer is "no, you can't". A good prompt and an ads connector get you surprisingly far.

What's harder is everything after that. Remembering what your last 2,000 ads taught you. Knowing which ones won because of the offer and which because of the creative. Not uploading company data somewhere you shouldn't.

That's where we spend most of our time.

If you're building it yourself, decide early where the memory lives. That's the bit that breaks first.
client_stories.source: Six brands raised it Aug-Nov 2026 (fashion, nutrition, apparel, skincare)

client_angles: A kids' nutrition brand was quoted a big fee for a 'Gujarat creator' whose audience was mostly outside Gujarat: check where the audience lives, not where the creator was born.
Brand fit written as checkable conditions (language, audience age, rival brands, past controversy) instead of a vibe.
We reviewed creator videos already live for a hair-care brand: most still had a fix pending (missing disclaimer, wrong term, wrong 'before' person). QC at 1,000 videos a month.
The real creator workflow in India: one WhatsApp group, one agency person, and five videos with no names on them.
A shirt brand found the best predictor of a winning creator video was whether the shirt was ironed: presentation beats script in fashion.
Media knows what works; design never hears it. Performance data sits in a weekly doc and never reaches the people making the next ad.
Comments are a weak signal now: people save and send instead. Most comments on fashion ads say nothing about buying.
Your top-ROAS creator list is mostly your retainer list: survivorship, not insight.
100 local creators in 8 languages at launch: who on the team actually watched all 100 drafts?
What the Meta Ad Library can and can't tell you about a competitor: no spend, dark ads, nobody deletes old ads.
A skincare team in Bangkok makes 15 videos a month with one person who shoots, edits and appears on camera; their competitor makes 80.
A global brand has an asset library nobody uploads to, because uploading gives them nothing back.
ig_news_ideas:
Weekly brief (fill on Tuesday of this week): pick the one or two Instagram or Meta changes from the last 7 days that matter to brands working with creators. Sources: Adam Mosseri's Instagram/Threads, @creators, Meta newsroom, TechCrunch, Social Media Today. Confirm each change on an official source. Structure: hook (the change, plainly), what it means for a brand or a creator campaign, one thing to do this week. Use a client question if one fits (no names). Close: Follow Galvor for what's new on Instagram every Thursday.
Ideas already raised by clients to use on slow weeks: Story layouts and fonts; Edits app on desktop and auto audio; Insights redesign; 'Your Algorithm' feed controls; trial reels for testing hooks; collab ads as the default way to boost creator posts; Instagram auto-translation vs regional briefs; long-form 'Features' test; originality rules for reposted content.
